subject: devops
subtopic: Dropping a column during a rolling deploy
question: Is dropping the column in the same release safe?

artifact.pipeline:
# Release 5.0: code stops using users.nickname; the migration drops the column.
# Pipeline: run migration, then rolling update of 6 pods (takes ~8 minutes).
# AI: "The new code doesn't use nickname, so dropping it in the same release is safe."

ai_claim: Yes. The new code no longer reads nickname, so removing the column in the same release causes no errors.

ai_solution.text: Release 5.0 stops using nickname.
The migration drops the column.
The new code does not need it.
So there are no errors.

failure.misconception: Forgetting old code runs during a rolling deploy
failure.explanation: The migration runs first, then pods are replaced over about 8 minutes. During that window, old pods (still selecting nickname) query a column that no longer exists and fail; a rollback would fail too. Use expand-and-contract: release 5.0 stops using the column, and a later release drops it once no old code remains.
failure.why_convincing: The new code really does not need the column.

canonical_solution: No: old pods still query nickname during the rollout. Drop the column in a later release.

valid_evidence.summary: migration drops nickname -> old pods: 'column users.nickname does not exist' for ~8 minutes
5.0: stop reading/writing nickname. 5.1 (after 5.0 is fully deployed): drop the column.

counterexamples: Requests served by old pods fail during the rollout.

hints.text: Ask which code versions run during the rollout.
Step 3 considers only the new code.
Schema changes must be compatible with old and new code at once.
Trace an old pod after the migration.
Step 3 is wrong: old pods still use the column. Use expand-and-contract.

repair: Split the change: stop using the column first, drop it in a later release.
debrief: During a rolling deploy, two versions run at once. Database changes must work for both.

subject: devops
question: Can the team reliably roll back to the previous version with this setup?

artifact.manifest:
containers:
  - name: web
    image: acme/web:latest
    imagePullPolicy: Always
# Rollback plan: "re-deploy the previous version."

ai_claim: Yes. They can re-deploy the previous version at any time, because the images are in the registry.

ai_solution.text: Every release is pushed to the registry.
Old images remain stored.
The team can re-deploy the previous one.
So rollback is reliable.

failure.explanation: The manifest references 'latest', which now points to the bad release. 'Re-deploy the previous version' has no identifier: nobody recorded which digest was running, and restarting pods pulls the same broken latest. Pods may even run different versions after a node restart. Deploy immutable version tags or digests (acme/web:2.7.3 or @sha256:...) and record each deployment.
failure.why_convincing: The previous image does exist somewhere in the registry.

canonical_solution: No: 'latest' is mutable and the previous version is not identified. Deploy immutable tags or digests.

valid_evidence.summary: rollout undo re-applies the previous ReplicaSet spec, which also says acme/web:latest -> pulls the broken image

counterexamples: Restarting pods pulls the broken 'latest' again.

hints.text: Ask what 'latest' points to after the bad release.
Step 3 assumes the previous version is identifiable.
Deployments need immutable references.
Try kubectl rollout undo.
Step 3 is wrong: latest is mutable. Use version tags or digests.

repair: Deploy immutable tags or digests and keep a deployment history.
debrief: Rollbacks need a precise target. Immutable references make 'the previous version' mean something.

subject: devops
question: Are no requests lost when pods are terminated during a deploy?

artifact.manifest:
# Pods are terminated during rolling updates.
# The app exits immediately on SIGTERM; no preStop hook; terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
# Some requests (report exports) take up to 20 seconds.
# AI: "Kubernetes stops sending traffic before terminating a pod, so no requests are lost."

ai_claim: Yes. Kubernetes removes a pod from the Service before stopping it, so no requests are lost.

ai_solution.text: Terminating pods are removed from Service endpoints.
So new requests go to other pods.
The pod is then stopped.
No requests are lost.

failure.misconception: Assuming endpoint removal and shutdown are coordinated
failure.explanation: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen concurrently; load balancers and kube-proxy take a moment to stop routing, so new requests can still arrive. And because the app exits immediately on SIGTERM, in-flight 20-second exports are cut off. Handle SIGTERM gracefully (stop accepting, finish in-flight work within the grace period), and add a short preStop delay so routing updates first.
failure.why_convincing: Removal from endpoints is real and happens early.

canonical_solution: No: the app aborts in-flight requests on SIGTERM, and routing updates race with shutdown. Add graceful shutdown and a preStop delay.

valid_evidence.summary: SIGTERM at t=0 -> app exits at t=0.1 s -> 15-second export in progress returns a connection reset
lifecycle: {preStop: {exec: {command: ["sleep", "5"]}}}  # plus: on SIGTERM stop accepting and drain for up to 25 s

counterexamples: Report exports in progress fail during each deploy.

hints.text: Ask what the app does on SIGTERM.
Step 4 ignores in-flight requests.
Graceful shutdown requires the app to drain work and routing to update first.
Trace an export running when SIGTERM arrives.
Step 4 is wrong: in-flight requests are killed. Drain gracefully.

repair: Implement graceful SIGTERM handling and a preStop delay within the grace period.
debrief: Zero-downtime deploys need cooperation from the app: stop taking work, finish what is in flight, then exit.

subject: devops
question: Does a clean 5-minute canary at 03:00 prove the release is safe?

artifact.pipeline:
canary:
  weight: 5%
  duration: 5m
  success: error_rate < 1%
# Scheduled for 03:00 IST, when traffic is ~40 requests/min.
# AI: "5 minutes of canary traffic with no errors proves the release is safe."

ai_claim: Yes. The canary served real traffic for 5 minutes without errors, which shows the release is safe to promote.

ai_solution.text: 5% of traffic went to the new version.
It ran for 5 minutes.
The error rate stayed below 1%.
So the release is safe.

failure.misconception: Assuming a tiny sample represents production
failure.explanation: At 40 requests/min, 5% for 5 minutes is about 10 requests - far too few to detect even a 5% error rate reliably (10 requests show no errors about 60% of the time at that rate), and night-time traffic misses daytime features and load. Size canaries by request count and cover representative traffic: run longer, at higher weight, or at peak, with statistical comparison to the baseline.
failure.why_convincing: Real production traffic sounds like strong evidence.

canonical_solution: No: about 10 requests cannot establish safety. Size the canary by traffic volume and duration.

valid_evidence.summary: canary: weight 10%, run until 5,000 requests or 60 minutes, compare error rate and p99 latency with baseline

counterexamples: A bug affecting 5% of requests is likely to show no errors in 10 requests.

hints.text: Count the requests the canary served.
Step 4 generalises from a tiny sample.
Canary analysis needs enough traffic to detect regressions.
Compute 40 x 5 x 0.05.
Step 4 is wrong: 10 requests prove little. Size canaries by volume.

repair: Run canaries on enough traffic (by count), compared statistically with the baseline.
debrief: A canary is an experiment. Without enough samples, 'no errors' is not evidence.

subject: devops
question: Is the AI right that this gives a near-instant, low-risk rollback path?

artifact.plan:
# Blue (v1) serves all traffic. Green (v2) is deployed alongside and passes smoke tests on an internal URL.
# The load balancer switches 100% of traffic to green; blue keeps running for 1 hour.
# If metrics degrade, traffic is switched back to blue.
# Database migrations in v2 are additive only (backward compatible).

ai_claim: Yes. Blue stays running and untouched, so rolling back is just switching the load balancer back; because v2's migrations are additive, v1 still works against the database.

ai_solution.text: Green is tested on an internal URL before receiving traffic.
The switch moves all traffic at once.
Blue remains running for an hour, ready to take traffic.
Additive migrations keep the database compatible with v1, so switching back works.

canonical_solution: Correct. Blue-green with backward-compatible schema changes gives an immediate rollback by traffic switch.

valid_evidence.summary: 14:05 switch to green; 14:12 error rate rises; 14:13 switch back to blue; errors stop

hints.text: Ask what makes rollback fast and safe here.
Step 4 addresses the database.
Rollback by traffic switch requires the old version to keep working with current data.
Consider what would break if a column had been dropped.
This solution is correct. The design supports instant rollback. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Fast rollbacks depend on keeping the old version runnable, including compatibility with the database.
